title: Iterator pipelines
summary: Lazy adapters compose left to right; nothing runs until a consumer like collect() drives it.
lecture: A slice or Vec is not an iterator — .iter() turns it into one (borrowing each element; into_iter() moves them, iter_mut() borrows mutably). Adapters like .filter() and .map() wrap the iterator and do nothing yet: they are lazy descriptions of work.

A consumer — .collect(), .sum(), a for loop — drives the pipeline, pulling elements through every stage in composition order. Order therefore changes meaning, not just style: filter-then-map processes fewer elements than map-then-filter, and if the map changes the property being filtered, the results differ too.

.collect() must come last, and its target type steers inference — Vec<i32>, String, HashMap — often via the function's return type. If the compiler complains it 'cannot infer type' mid-pipeline, something after collect() is trying to keep iterating a finished collection.
The idiomatic payoff: pipelines replace hand-written loops with no index juggling, no mutable accumulator, and equal or better performance.

example.code:
let evens_doubled: Vec<i32> = values
    .iter()
    .filter(|x| *x % 2 == 0)   // keep evens FIRST
    .map(|x| x * 2)            // then double them
    .collect();
example.caption: Swap filter and map and every doubled number is even — the test catches it.
